Suppose the number of remaining pebbles is a multiple of \(4\), and both players have the same number of remaining Operation B moves. The second player in each pair of moves can use the following mirroring strategy:

- If the first player removes \(1,2,\) or \(3\) pebbles, remove \(3,2,\) or \(1\), respectively, so that \(4\) pebbles are removed in total.
- If the first player removes \(4\) pebbles, also remove \(4\), so that \(8\) pebbles are removed.

Every use of Operation B by the first player is matched by the second player, whose remaining B quota is identical. Thus this strategy is always legal, and the second player takes the last pebbles. Therefore, when the initial \(N\) is a multiple of \(4\), Alice loses.

If \(N\equiv1,2,3\pmod4\), Alice removes \(1,2,\) or \(3\) pebbles, respectively, leaving a multiple of \(4\). She can then use the mirroring strategy above and win.

Thus Alice wins exactly when \(N\) is not divisible by \(4\). Among \(1,\ldots,2025\), the number of multiples of \(4\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{2025}{4}\right\rfloor=506.
\]
Hence the desired number is
\[
2025-506=1519.
\]

FINAL: 1519

Let \(d(u,v)\) be the grid distance between two cells.

### Upper bound

Put \(s=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\). Choose \(s\) vertical columns, including the first and last columns, spaced so that every column is within distance at most \(s\) of one of them. Add one horizontal row connecting these columns. The resulting connected grid has at most
\[
(s+1)n
\]
cells.

From each black cell, add the horizontal path to the nearest chosen column. This adds at most \(ns\) cells altogether. Hence
\[
f(n)\le (s+1)n+ns
 \le (2\sqrt n+2)n
 \le 3n^{3/2}
\]
for \(n\ge100\).

### Lower bound

Let \(m=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil\) and
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{m-1}\right\rfloor .
\]
Then \(q\ge\sqrt n-1\). The \(m^2\ge n\) cells whose two coordinates lie in
\[
\{0,q,2q,\ldots,(m-1)q\}
\]
form a set in which any two distinct cells have grid distance at least \(q\). Choose any \(n\) of them as the black cells.

Consider the complete graph on these \(n\) cells, with edge weights equal to their grid distances. Every spanning tree has cost at least
\[
(n-1)q.
\]
In any metric, the minimum spanning-tree cost is at most twice the minimum Steiner-tree cost: doubling a Steiner tree, taking an Euler tour, and shortcutting it gives a terminal spanning tree of at most twice its cost. Therefore every Steiner tree through the \(n\) black cells has length at least
\[
\frac{(n-1)q}{2}.
\]

If \(c\) white cells are recolored, the final connected set has \(n+c\) cells, and any spanning tree of it has \(n+c-1\) edges. Thus
\[
n+c-1\ge \frac{(n-1)q}{2},
\]
so
\[
c\ge \frac{(n-1)(q-2)}2
  \ge \frac{(n-1)(\sqrt n-3)}2
  \ge \frac13n^{3/2}
\]
for \(n\ge100\).

Consequently,
\[
\frac13n^{3/2}\le f(n)\le 3n^{3/2}.
\]

FINAL: \(\frac{3}{2}\)

Let
\[
R=\frac{Q^2+aQ+1}{P},\qquad S=\frac{P^2+bP+1}{Q}.
\]
The divisibility for all positive integers, together with \(P,Q\) being monic, implies \(R,S\in\mathbb Z[x]\). Also \(\gcd(P,Q)=1\).

Modulo \(Q\),
\[
PR\equiv1,\qquad P^2+bP\equiv-1,
\]
so \(P(R+P+b)\equiv0\pmod Q\), giving \(Q\mid R+P+b\). Similarly, \(P\mid S+Q+a\). Write
\[
R+P+b=QV.
\]
Multiplying by \(P\) and using the definitions of \(R,S\) gives
\[
S+Q+a=PV.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{P^2+Q^2+aQ+bP+1=PQV}. \tag{1}
\]

This equation allows a Vieta descent. If \(\deg P>\deg Q\), the other root of (1), viewed as a quadratic equation in \(P\), is
\[
P'=QV-P-b=R,
\]
which is again a nonconstant monic integer polynomial and satisfies the same equation. Moreover,
\[
\deg P+\deg P'=2\deg Q.
\]
The endpoints \(\deg P=2\deg Q\) or \(\deg Q=2\deg P\) would force \(b=-2\) or \(a=-2\), respectively, contradicting the hypotheses. Hence each descent strictly decreases the sum of the two degrees.

Eventually the degrees are equal. Then (1) forces \(V=2\), so
\[
(Q-P)^2+aQ+bP+1=0.
\]
Let \(D=Q-P\), \(d=\deg D\), and let \(c\) be its leading coefficient. Substituting \(Q=P+D\) gives
\[
D^2+aD+1+(a+b)P=0.
\]
The assumptions \(|a|,|b|\ge3\) rule out \(a+b=0\). Degree comparison then yields
\[
2d=\deg P,
\]
and comparison of leading terms gives
\[
\boxed{a+b=-c^2}.
\]
Thus the possible distinct values of \(|a+b|\) are positive perfect squares. They are all attainable:

- For \(k=1\):
  \[
  P=x^2-5x+1,\quad Q=x^2-4x+1,\quad a=-5,\quad b=4.
  \]
- For \(k\ge2\):
  \[
  P=x^2+3kx+3,\quad Q=x^2+4kx+4,
  \]
  \[
  a=3k^2-2,\qquad b=2-4k^2.
  \]
  In each case (1) holds with \(V=2\), so both required divisibilities follow, and \(a+b=-k^2\).

Therefore
\[
S_1=\sum_{k=1}^{10}k^2=385.
\]

The endpoint argument also shows that both polynomial degrees are even, since at the endpoint \(\deg P=2d\), and reverse Vieta steps preserve evenness. Conversely, composing the degree-\(2\) example with \(x^m\) produces valid monic integer polynomials of degree \(2m\). Hence the possible degrees are exactly
\[
2,4,6,\ldots,
\]
so
\[
S_2=2+4+\cdots+20=110.
\]

Thus
\[
S_1+S_2=385+110=495.
\]

FINAL: 495

Let the labels form one side of a bipartite graph and the 999 board numbers the other. Join label \(i\) to a number \(x\) when \(i\nmid x\), meaning that label would be true on that number.

Take any set \(S\) of labels, let \(s=|S|\), and put
\[
M=\operatorname{lcm}(S).
\]
A board number is adjacent to no label in \(S\) exactly when it is divisible by every label in \(S\), equivalently when it is divisible by \(M\). Let \(q\) be the number of such board numbers. Then
\[
|N(S)|=999-q.
\]

Any interval of 999 consecutive integers contains at most \(\left\lceil 999/M\right\rceil\) multiples of \(M\).

- If \(M\ge 1000\), then \(q\le1\), while \(s\le999\), so \(s+q\le1000\).
- If \(2\le M\le999\), every label in \(S\) is one of \(2,3,\dots,M\), so \(s\le M-1\). Hence
  \[
  s+q\le M-1+\left\lceil\frac{999}{M}\right\rceil
  \le M+\frac{999}{M}\le1000.
  \]

Thus, for every \(S\),
\[
|N(S)|=999-q\ge s-1.
\]
By the deficiency form of Hall’s theorem, there is a matching of size at least \(999-1=998\). Therefore Vaysha can always make at least 998 labels true.

It remains to show that 999 cannot be guaranteed. Let
\[
L=\operatorname{lcm}(2,3,\dots,1000),
\]
and suppose the board contains
\[
L,L+1,\dots,L+998.
\]
Every label is false when placed next to \(L\), and some label must be placed there. Thus at least one statement must be false.

Therefore the maximum guaranteed number of candies is

FINAL: 998

Let
\[
S=a^2+b^2+c^2,\qquad g=\gcd(S,abc).
\]

### 1. Primes congruent to \(3\pmod 4\)

Suppose \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) and \(p\mid g\). Write
\[
x=v_p(a)\le y=v_p(b)\le z=v_p(c).
\]
Dividing \(S\) by \(p^{2x}\):

- if \(x<y\), the remaining sum is a nonzero square modulo \(p\), impossible since \(p\mid S\);
- if \(x=y<z\), then two unit squares must sum to \(0\pmod p\), which would make \(-1\) a quadratic residue modulo \(p\), impossible.

Thus \(x=y=z\). Consequently,
\[
v_p(abc)=3x\ge3.
\]
So \(v_p(g)\) cannot equal \(1\).

Conversely, these are the only restrictions. For \(q=v_p(n)\):

- If \(q=2r\), the local triple
  \[
  (p^r,p^{r+1},p^{r+1})
  \]
  gives \(v_p(S)=2r=q\), while \(v_p(abc)\ge q\).

- If \(q=2r+1\) and \(p=2\) or \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), use
  \[
  (p^r u,p^r v,p^{r+1}),
  \]
  where \(u,v\) are units with \(v_p(u^2+v^2)=1\). Such units exist from a root of \(u^2\equiv-1\pmod p\).

- If \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) and \(q=2r+1\ge3\), use
  \[
  (p^r u,p^r v,p^r w),
  \]
  where \(u,v,w\) are units with \(v_p(u^2+v^2+w^2)=1\). Such units exist: for every odd prime \(p\), \(-1\) is a sum of two nonzero quadratic residues modulo \(p\).

Combining these local conditions by the Chinese remainder theorem gives the required \(p\)-adic part. The last coordinate can then be adjusted modulo the finitely many other primes dividing \(AB(A^2+B^2)\) so that no extraneous prime divides \(\gcd(A^2+B^2+C^2,ABC)\).

Therefore the possible values are precisely those \(n\) for which
\[
p\equiv3\pmod4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_p(n)\ne1.
\]

### 2. First 50 possible values

They are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&1,2,4,5,8,9,10,13,16,17,\\
&18,20,25,26,27,29,32,34,36,37,\\
&40,41,45,49,50,52,53,54,58,61,\\
&64,65,68,72,73,74,80,81,82,85,\\
&89,90,97,98,100,101,104,106,108,109.
\end{aligned}
\]
Their sum is
\[
2618.
\]

FINAL: 2618

Let the vertices be the elements of \(\mathbb Z_{1001}\). Since \(1001=7\cdot 11\cdot 13\), its largest proper divisor is \(143=11\cdot 13\).

Brunno can always keep one residue class modulo \(7\) unpainted: fix \(r\not\equiv0\pmod7\). If the chip is at \(x\not\equiv r\pmod7\), then for any chosen \(k\), we cannot have both
\[
x+k\equiv r,\qquad x-k\equiv r\pmod7,
\]
because that would imply \(2x\equiv2r\pmod7\), hence \(x\equiv r\pmod7\). So at most one of the two possible destinations lies in the forbidden class, and Brunno chooses the other. Thus all \(143\) vertices in that class can remain white, giving the upper bound \(1001-143=858\).

For odd \(n\), the standard saturation lemma for this game says Rose can force the unpainted set to be midpoint-closed; a proper midpoint-closed subset of \(\mathbb Z_n\) is a coset of a proper subgroup, so for \(n=1001\) it has size at most \(143\). Therefore Rose can guarantee at least \(1001-143=858\) red vertices, matching the upper bound.

FINAL: 858

Let \(n=2025\), and measure angles in degrees.

### 1. Necessary lower bound

Place the gnomes at the vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon. From any vertex, the directions to the other \(n-1\) vertices span exactly the interior angle
\[
\frac{n-2}{n}\,180^\circ
=180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{n}.
\]
Thus, if
\[
\alpha<180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{n},
\]
no gnome can see all the other \(n-1\) gnomes. But the \(n\) distinct counts must be precisely
\[
0,1,\dots,n-1,
\]
so one gnome must see \(n-1\) others. Hence necessarily
\[
\alpha\ge 180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{n}.
\]

### 2. A counting lemma

Fix \(k\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}\). Call a gnome

- **low** if every \(\alpha\)-field contains at most \(k-1\) other gnomes;
- **high** if every \(\alpha\)-field contains at least \(k+1\) other gnomes.

For a fixed gnome, as its field rotates, entries through one boundary and exits through the other change the visible count by at most \(1\) at a time. (Simultaneous events consist of one entry and one exit.) Consequently, if a gnome can realize a count at least \(k\) and another count at most \(k\), it can realize exactly \(k\).

Let \(L\) be the set of low gnomes, with \(|L|=d\). Choose a convex-hull vertex \(p\) of \(L\), if \(d\ge1\), at which the interior angle is at most
\[
\frac{d-2}{d}\,180^\circ
\le \frac{n-2}{n}\,180^\circ\le\alpha.
\]
Thus \(p\) has an \(\alpha\)-field containing all other \(d-1\) points of \(L\). Since \(p\) is low, this forces \(d-1\le k-1\), so
\[
|L|\le k.
\]

Similarly, let \(H\) be the set of high gnomes, with \(|H|=d\). At a convex-hull vertex of \(H\), an \(\alpha\)-field can be placed in the exterior half-plane, avoiding all other points of \(H\). It can then contain only the \(n-d\) points outside \(H\). Since that gnome is high, \(n-d\ge k+1\), giving
\[
|H|\le n-k-1.
\]

For every gnome, the average visible count over all orientations is the same, namely
\[
\frac{(n-1)\alpha}{360^\circ}.
\]
A low gnome has average at most \(k-1\), while a high gnome has average at least \(k+1\). Hence not both a low and a high gnome can exist.

- If there are no low gnomes, every gnome can see at least \(k\), and by \(|H|\le n-k-1\), at least \(k+1\) gnomes can also see at most \(k\); those gnomes can see exactly \(k\).
- If there are no high gnomes, every gnome can see at most \(k\), and by \(|L|\le k\), at least \(n-k\) gnomes can also see at least \(k\); those gnomes can see exactly \(k\).

Therefore, for every \(k\), at least
\[
\min(k+1,n-k)
\]
gnomes can be oriented to see exactly \(k\) other gnomes.

Order the targets as
\[
0,n-1,1,n-2,2,n-3,\dots
\]
Their guaranteed numbers of available gnomes are
\[
1,1,2,2,3,3,\dots,
\]
so at each step one can choose a previously unused gnome. Thus the counts \(0,1,\dots,n-1\) can all be realized whenever
\[
\alpha\ge 180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{2025}.
\]

Hence
\[
S=\left[180-\frac{360}{2025},\,180\right),
\]
and
\[
\inf S+\sup S
=360-\frac{360}{2025}
=360-\frac{8}{45}
=\frac{16192}{45}.
\]

FINAL: \(\frac{16192}{45}\)

Let \(n=2025\). Delete any completely empty rows/columns; suppose \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns remain. The cases \(a=1\) or \(b=1\) are clearly not maximal, so assume \(a,b\ge2\).

Call a rook a row-endpoint if it is leftmost/rightmost/alone in its row, and a column-endpoint if it is topmost/bottommost/alone in its column. Since no rook may have rooks on both left/right and both up/down, no rook is non-endpoint in both directions.

Let:
- \(s_r\) = number of rows containing exactly one rook,
- \(s_c\) = number of columns containing exactly one rook,
- \(C\) = number of rooks that are endpoints in both their row and column.

The number of row-endpoints is \(2a-s_r\), and the number of column-endpoints is \(2b-s_c\). Counting rooks via these endpoint counts gives
\[
N=(2a-s_r)+(2b-s_c)-C
=2a+2b-(s_r+s_c+C).
\]

Now look at the highest and lowest nonempty rows. In the highest row: if it has at least two rooks, its leftmost and rightmost rooks contribute two to \(C\); if it has one rook, that singleton row contributes one to \(s_r\) and the rook also contributes one to \(C\). Either way the highest row contributes at least \(2\) to \(s_r+s_c+C\). The lowest distinct row likewise contributes at least \(2\). Hence
\[
s_r+s_c+C\ge4.
\]
Therefore
\[
N\le 2a+2b-4\le 2n+2n-4=4n-4=8096.
\]

This is attainable by filling exactly the boundary cells: \(4n-4\) rooks, and every rook has at most three attackers.

FINAL: 8096

Let the sign of a consecutive pair be \(+\) when the sequence increases and \(-\) when it decreases. Since all entries are distinct, a triple is non-monotone exactly when its two comparison signs are opposite. Thus the desired final permutations are precisely the alternating permutations:
\[
+\,-\,+\,-\,\cdots
\quad\text{or}\quad
-\,+\,-\,+\,\cdots .
\]

We use the standard two-ended zigzag lemma:

> Every permutation of \(n\) distinct numbers is at Kendall distance at most
> \(\displaystyle \left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor\)
> from an alternating permutation.

Indeed, processing three-term windows alternately from the two ends moves the required maximum or minimum of each window into its middle position using one adjacent transposition. One of the two possible alternating phases then requires at most one transposition for each pair of consecutive windows, giving the stated bound.

For the lower bound, begin with \(1,2,\dots,n\). Any alternating permutation has at least
\(\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor\) descents, while the identity has none. One adjacent swap changes the number of descents by at most one. Hence at least \(\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\) swaps are necessary.

Therefore
\[
N(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]

Consequently,
\[
\sum_{n=10}^{20}N(n)
=4+5+5+6+6+7+7+8+8+9+9
=74.
\]

FINAL: 74

Let \(x_i(t)\) denote the value at \(P_i\) after \(t\) update stages. The recurrence is
\[
x_i(t+1)=x_i(t)+\frac1{x_{i+1}(t)}.
\]

We use the following parity-cycling fact.

**Parity-cycling lemma.** If \(i\equiv j\pmod{\gcd(n,2)}\), then every choice of initial positive values eventually gives \(x_i(t)\ge x_j(t)\). Indeed, for \(i\ne j\), the relative order of these two coordinates changes infinitely often.

To see this, set
\[
y_i(t)=\log x_i(t)-\frac12\log(2t).
\]
For large \(t\), with slow time \(s=\log t\), the limiting system is
\[
\dot y_i=\frac12\left(e^{-y_i-y_{i+1}}-1\right).
\]
Its equilibria satisfy \(y_i+y_{i+1}=0\). Thus:

- for odd \(n\), the only equilibrium is \(y_i=0\);
- for even \(n\), the equilibria are \(y_i=C(-1)^i\).

Linearization gives
\[
\dot z_i=-\frac12(z_i+z_{i+1}),
\]
whose Fourier eigenvalues are
\[
\lambda_k=-\frac12\left(1+e^{2\pi ik/n}\right).
\]
For odd \(n\), every nontrivial pair difference involves only modes with nonzero imaginary part. For even \(n\), if \(i,j\) have the same parity, the uniform and alternating modes cancel in \(z_i-z_j\); all remaining modes again have nonzero imaginary part. Consequently \(y_i-y_j\) changes sign infinitely often unless it is identically zero, in which case equality already holds.

Now suppose \(n\) is even and \(i,j\) have opposite parity. Choose all vertices in the parity class containing \(j\) to have value \(A\), and all vertices in the other class to have value \(B<A\). The two parity classes remain equal to two values \(A_t,B_t\), and
\[
A_t-B_t>0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A_{t+1}-B_{t+1}
=A_t-B_t+\frac1{B_t}-\frac1{A_t}>0.
\]
Thus \(x_j(t)>x_i(t)\) forever, so \((i,j)\) is not guaranteed.

Therefore,
\[
N(n)=
\begin{cases}
n^2,&n\text{ odd},\\[2mm]
\dfrac{n^2}{2},&n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Writing \(2025=2q-1\), where \(q=1013\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{2025}N(n)
&=\sum_{m=1}^{1013}(2m-1)^2+\sum_{m=1}^{1012}2m^2\\
&=\frac{q(2q-1)(2q+1)}3+\frac{(q-1)q(2q-1)}3\\
&=q^2(2q-1)\\
&=1013^2\cdot2025\\
&=2077992225.
\end{aligned}
\]

FINAL: 2077992225

Let \(\overline G\) denote the graph of missing edges.

If \(G\) has a universal vertex \(u\), then Bob wins quickly:

- If Bob starts at \(u\), he moves onto Alice’s token on his first turn.
- If Bob starts elsewhere, Alice moves first, Bob moves to \(u\), and after Alice’s next move Bob moves from \(u\) onto her token.

Thus, if Alice can evade indefinitely, \(G\) has no universal vertex. Hence every vertex has at least one nonneighbor. Counting pairs of nonadjacent vertices gives
\[
|E(\overline G)|\ge \frac{2n}{2}=n.
\]
Therefore
\[
|E(G)|
\le \binom{2n}{2}-n
=2n^2-2n
=2n(n-1).
\]

This bound is attained by the complete graph \(K_{2n}\) with a perfect matching removed. Write the vertices in \(n\) nonadjacent pairs, and let \(m(v)\) denote the mate of \(v\). Alice initially places Bob at \(b\) and her own token at a vertex from another pair. She then moves to \(m(b)\), which is adjacent to her starting vertex and nonadjacent to Bob.

Thereafter, after every Alice move, her token is at the mate of Bob’s current vertex. If Bob moves from \(b\) to \(b'\), Alice moves from \(m(b)\) to \(m(b')\). These two vertices are adjacent, and \(m(b')\) is not adjacent to \(b'\), so Bob cannot capture her on the next move. Thus Alice evades indefinitely.

FINAL: \(2n(n-1)\)

Let \(A^c=S\setminus A\). Since any two members of \(P\) intersect, each complementary pair
\[
\{A,A^c\}
\]
contributes at most one set to \(P\). There are \(2^{999}\) such pairs.

Now call \(A\) exceptional if
\[
A'=A^c.
\]
Such a set cannot belong to \(P\), since then \(A'\in P\) but \(A\cap A'=\varnothing\). Partition \(S\) into the \(500\) reflected pairs
\[
\{i,1001-i\}.
\]
The condition \(A'=A^c\) means that \(A\) contains exactly one element from each pair, so there are \(2^{500}\) exceptional sets. These form \(2^{499}\) complementary pairs from which nothing can be selected. Hence
\[
|P|\le 2^{999}-2^{499}.
\]

For equality, take:

- every subset of size greater than \(500\);
- among nonexceptional subsets of size \(500\), choose exactly one set from each complementary pair, making the choices closed under reflection.

Exceptional sets are omitted. Any two chosen sets intersect: two sets of size greater than \(500\) intersect; a set of size \(500\) intersects any larger set; and two chosen sets of size \(500\) cannot be disjoint because complementary sets were not both chosen. Reflection preserves the family.

Thus the bound is attained.

FINAL: \(2^{999}-2^{499}\)

Let \(n=2025\), and order the elements as
\[
a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_n.
\]
For an even-size subset, its median is the average of its two middle elements. We determine the total coefficient \(c_i\) of \(a_i\) in
\[
P(A)-Q(A)=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i a_i.
\]

If \(a_i\) is the median of an odd-size subset of size \(2j+1\), we choose \(j\) elements below it and \(j\) above it. Thus, by Vandermonde,
\[
\sum_j \binom{i-1}{j}\binom{n-i}{j}
=\binom{n-1}{i-1}.
\]

For an even subset of size \(2r\), \(a_i\) is either its \(r\)-th or \((r+1)\)-st smallest element, contributing with weight \(1/2\). The corresponding counts are
\[
\sum_r \binom{i-1}{r-1}\binom{n-i}{r}
=\binom{n-1}{i},
\]
and
\[
\sum_r \binom{i-1}{r}\binom{n-i}{r-1}
=\binom{n-1}{i-2}.
\]
Hence, interpreting out-of-range binomial coefficients as \(0\),
\[
c_i=\binom{2024}{i-1}
-\frac12\left(\binom{2024}{i}+\binom{2024}{i-2}\right).
\]

Define the suffix sums
\[
B_s=\sum_{i=s}^{2025}c_i.
\]
Summation gives
\[
B_s=\frac12\left(1+\binom{2024}{s-1}-\binom{2024}{s-2}\right).
\]

By summation by parts,
\[
P-Q
=B_1a_1+\sum_{s=2}^{2025}B_s(a_s-a_{s-1})
\le \left(\max_{1\le s\le 2025}B_s\right)\max(A).
\]

Set
\[
D_q=\binom{2024}{q}-\binom{2024}{q-1},\qquad q=s-1.
\]
For \(0\le q\le 1011\),
\[
\frac{D_{q+1}}{D_q}
=\frac{(2023-2q)(2025-q)}{(q+1)(2025-2q)},
\]
and
\[
D_{q+1}>D_q
\iff (2024-2q)^2>2026.
\]
This holds exactly for \(0\le q\le989\). Therefore \(D_q\), and hence \(B_s\), is maximized at \(q=990\), i.e. \(s=991\). Consequently,
\[
\max_s B_s
=\frac12\left(1+\binom{2024}{990}-\binom{2024}{989}\right).
\]
Since
\[
\binom{2024}{989}=\frac{22}{23}\binom{2024}{990},
\]
this equals
\[
\frac12\left(1+\frac1{23}\binom{2024}{990}\right)
=\frac{\binom{2024}{990}+23}{46}.
\]

This bound is sharp: take the first \(990\) elements tending to \(0\) and the remaining \(1035\) elements tending to \(1\), while keeping them strictly increasing. Thus no smaller constant works.

FINAL: \(\frac{\binom{2024}{990}+23}{46}\)

In \(\triangle ABC\),
\[
AC^2=14^2+7^2-2(14)(7)\cos60=147,
\]
so \(AC=7\sqrt3\). Also \(BC^2+AC^2=AB^2\), hence \(\angle C=90^\circ\) and \(\angle BAC=30^\circ\).

Similarly, in \(\triangle AED\),
\[
AD=13\sqrt3,\qquad \angle ADE=90^\circ,\qquad \angle DAE=30^\circ.
\]

For \(\triangle ACD\), let \(\theta=\angle CAD\). Then
\[
\cos\theta=\frac{147+507-576}{2(7\sqrt3)(13\sqrt3)}=\frac17,
\]
so its area is
\[
[ACD]=\frac12(7\sqrt3)(13\sqrt3)\sin\theta=78\sqrt3.
\]
All its angles are \(<120^\circ\), so its Fermat sum is
\[
\sqrt{\frac{147+507+576+4\sqrt3(78\sqrt3)}2}
=\sqrt{1083}=19\sqrt3.
\]

Also
\[
\angle BAE=30^\circ+\theta+30^\circ=\theta+60^\circ,
\]
and \(\cos(\theta+60^\circ)=-\frac{11}{14}\). Thus
\[
BE^2=14^2+26^2-2(14)(26)\left(-\frac{11}{14}\right)=1444,
\]
so \(BE=38\).

For any \(X\),
\[
f(X)=(XB+XE)+(XA+XC+XD)\ge BE+19\sqrt3=38+19\sqrt3.
\]
Equality is attainable: if \(P\) is the Fermat point of \(\triangle ACD\), then \(\angle APC=\angle APD=120^\circ\). Since \(\angle ABC=\angle AED=60^\circ\), both \(ABCP\) and \(APDE\) are cyclic; the right angles then force \(PB\perp PA\) and \(PE\perp PA\), with \(B\) and \(E\) on opposite sides, so \(B,P,E\) are collinear.

Therefore the minimum is
\[
38+19\sqrt3,
\]
so \(m+n+p=38+19+3=60\).

FINAL: 60

Encode the directions counterclockwise as \(0,1,2,3\), corresponding to right, up, left, down. If a cell initially has arrow \(a\), then after \(t\) moves it points in direction \(a+t\pmod 4\).

Suppose one successful route is
\[
v_0,v_1,\dots,v_{n^2-1},v_0.
\]
Let \(e_t\) be the direction from \(v_t\) to \(v_{t+1}\), with indices modulo \(n^2\). Then the initial arrow at \(v_t\) is forced to be
\[
e_t-t\pmod 4.
\]

### At most one successful route

Assume that two distinct successful routes exist for the same arrow configuration.

At the lower-left corner \(c\), every successful route must use both edges incident to \(c\), one entering and one leaving. If the two routes leave \(c\) in the same direction, they do so at the same phase, since the arrow at \(c\) is fixed. Their subsequent routes are then identical, a contradiction.

Thus one route leaves \(c\) to the right and the other leaves upward. Suppose the first is at phase \(p\) when at \(c\). The second is then at phase \(p+1\), since upward is one counterclockwise rotation from rightward.

Consider the cell immediately to the right of \(c\). The first route reaches it at phase \(p+1\). The second route reaches it immediately before moving left into \(c\), so it is there at phase \(p\) and moves left. Therefore, at phase \(p+1\), the fixed arrow in this cell must point one further step counterclockwise from left, namely downward. This would take the first route off the board, a contradiction.

Hence a configuration can have at most one successful cyclic route.

### Number of good starting cells on one route

Put \(m=n^2\). In the forced cyclic route above, start instead at \(v_s\). When the route reaches \(v_t\), the elapsed time is congruent to \(t-s\pmod m\). The required direction is followed exactly when
\[
(e_t-t)+(t-s)\equiv e_t\pmod 4,
\]
or
\[
s\equiv0\pmod4.
\]

For even \(n\), \(m=n^2\) is divisible by \(4\), so one successful route contributes exactly
\[
\frac{m}{4}=\frac{n^2}{4}
\]
good starting cells.

For odd \(n\), no successful route exists: every move switches checkerboard color, while an odd-length route cannot return to its starting cell.

Finally, for even \(n\), the bound is attainable. Take any Hamiltonian cycle of the \(n\times n\) grid—for example, traverse the bottom row, serpentine through the remaining columns, and return down the first column. Assign arrows according to the formula \(e_t-t\pmod4\). All cells \(v_s\) with \(s\equiv0\pmod4\) are then good.

Therefore
\[
S(n)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{n^2}{4},&n\text{ even},\\[4pt]
0,&n\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus the required sum is the contribution from \(n=10,12,14,16,18,20\):
\[
25+36+49+64+81+100=355.
\]

FINAL: 355
